title: Nvidia Just Delivered Bad News for AMD and Intel

questions.question: What revenue will NVIDIA report from stand-alone CPUs for FY2028?
questions.why_it_matters: Stand-alone CPU revenue is a developing product line that could become a material source of NVIDIA growth and take share from established CPU vendors. Its scale would help show whether the agentic-AI opportunity is translating into sales.
questions.why_not_already_covered: The existing questions cover NVIDIA stand-alone CPU revenue for FY2027 and stand-alone server CPU revenue for calendar 2026 and FY2028. Those periods or scopes do not answer FY2028 stand-alone CPU revenue; this is a distinct annual product-revenue outcome.
questions.how_and_when_to_check: Check NVIDIA’s FY2028 annual results and annual report, expected around February 2028, for revenue attributed to stand-alone CPUs. The article does not state an exact publication date, and its FY2028 figure is management’s outlook, not reported revenue.

evidence.quote: Additionally, Kress said last quarter that they were projecting $20 billion in CPU sales for fiscal year 2027, which ends in late January.
evidence.what_it_shows: The article attributes a FY2027 CPU-sales projection to CFO Colette Kress, establishing a comparison point for the later outlook; it does not establish FY2028 realized sales.
evidence.original_speaker: NVIDIA CFO Colette Kress, as reported by the article

evidence.quote: The bad news for AMD and Intel is that Kress said Nvidia not only still expects $20 billion in CPU revenue in its fiscal 2027, but expects that number to more than double in fiscal 2028.
evidence.what_it_shows: The article reports Kress’s expectation that NVIDIA’s CPU revenue will more than double from the $20 billion FY2027 outlook in FY2028. This is a forecast, not a reported result, and supports tracking the eventual FY2028 revenue outcome.
evidence.original_speaker: NVIDIA CFO Colette Kress, as reported by the article

evidence.quote: Last quarter, the company surprised the market by introducing its stand-alone Vera CPU, specifically for running AI agents.
evidence.what_it_shows: The new stand-alone Vera CPU is the product context for the CPU-sales outlook and the article’s claim that NVIDIA is entering a market served by AMD and Intel.

evidence.quote: Nvidia says its CPUs can complete agentic tasks 1.8 times faster than industry standards and provide fivefold the bandwidth per watt than any other data center CPU .
evidence.what_it_shows: NVIDIA claims a performance and efficiency advantage that could support demand, though these are company claims rather than independent verification.
evidence.original_speaker: NVIDIA, as reported by the article

evidence.quote: Agentic AI continues to gain momentum. People can now use AI to deploy autonomous agents that can complete tasks with very little human interaction.
evidence.what_it_shows: The author identifies the broader adoption of agentic AI as a demand driver for CPU orchestration workloads.

evidence.quote: GPUs still handle most AI inference, but CPUs are now seen as the better option for orchestrating agentic workflows, such as calling tools and coordinating steps between model calls.
evidence.what_it_shows: The article’s explanation of CPUs’ role in agentic workloads provides a logical demand driver for NVIDIA’s stand-alone CPU revenue.

evidence.quote: This has led to CPU companies, such as AMD and Intel, to perform incredibly well, as demand for CPUs goes through the roof.
evidence.what_it_shows: The author describes strong CPU demand and competitive activity, supporting the potential market opportunity while indicating that NVIDIA faces established competitors.

evidence.quote: In a research report earlier this month, Bank of America analyst Vivek Arya once again raised his estimates for the total addressable market (TAM) for server CPUs.
evidence.what_it_shows: The article reports an analyst’s view that the addressable server-CPU market is expanding, an indirect driver of potential NVIDIA CPU sales.
evidence.original_speaker: Bank of America analyst Vivek Arya, as reported by the article

evidence.quote: A few months ago, Arya expected the TAM to grow by fivefold to $170 billion by 2030.
evidence.what_it_shows: Arya’s earlier estimate supplies context for the revised market outlook; it is an analyst estimate, not a realized market size.
evidence.original_speaker: Bank of America analyst Vivek Arya, as reported by the article

evidence.quote: Now, his new estimate is $210 billion, due to the rise of AI agents.
evidence.what_it_shows: Arya’s revised $210 billion server-CPU TAM estimate links expected market expansion to AI agents. It is a third-party forecast and does not establish NVIDIA’s eventual revenue.
evidence.original_speaker: Bank of America analyst Vivek Arya, as reported by the article

questions_written.question: What revenue will NVIDIA report from stand-alone CPUs for FY2028?

article:
Nvidia ( NVDA +2.53% ) recently delivered blowout second-quarter earnings that the market couldn't ignore, even if long-term questions about artificial intelligence (AI) remain.
The company easily beat Wall Street consensus estimates and raised third-quarter guidance beyond Street expectations. But the real kicker came when Nvidia CFO Colette Kress said that Nvidia is expecting 70% annual revenue growth in fiscal 2028, when the Street had only modeled 44%.
During the earnings call, management also discussed a newer, fast-growing business. It's bad news for Advanced Micro Devices ( AMD +3.09% ) and Intel ( INTC +5.71% ) .
Nvidia taking full advantage of agentic AI
Agentic AI continues to gain momentum. People can now use AI to deploy autonomous agents that can complete tasks with very little human interaction.
While graphics processing units (GPUs) have always been at the center of the AI story because they power the inference that trains large language models (LLMs), there's been a resurgence of central processing units (CPUs), the chips used to power legacy technology like cellphones and computers.
GPUs still handle most AI inference, but CPUs are now seen as the better option for orchestrating agentic workflows, such as calling tools and coordinating steps between model calls. This has led to CPU companies, such as AMD and Intel, to perform incredibly well, as demand for CPUs goes through the roof.
Unfortunately for Intel and AMD, this is also a business that was not hard for Nvidia to move into. Last quarter, the company surprised the market by introducing its stand-alone Vera CPU, specifically for running AI agents. Nvidia says its CPUs can complete agentic tasks 1.8 times faster than industry standards and provide fivefold the bandwidth per watt than any other data center CPU .
Additionally, Kress said last quarter that they were projecting $20 billion in CPU sales for fiscal year 2027, which ends in late January. That instantly made Nvidia competitive with other CPU leaders, such as AMD and Intel. In the second quarter, Intel reported $6.3 billion of data center and AI revenue, which is where CPU sales are categorized, although not broken out. AMD reported roughly $6.7 billion in data center revenue in the second quarter. It also does not break out CPU revenue individually.
The bad news for AMD and Intel is that Kress said Nvidia not only still expects $20 billion in CPU revenue in its fiscal 2027, but expects that number to more than double in fiscal 2028.
The good news is that agentic AI is likely to keep growing
If there's a silver lining for AMD and Intel, it's that agentic AI is likely to keep growing exponentially.
"Today, the vast majority of AI is prompted by people. I believe that this last month it has crossed. Most AI are now agentic," Nvidia's CEO Jensen Huang said on the company's earnings call. "But in the future, every company will have a whole bunch of agents. We have 40,000 employees, roughly. In the future, we'll have 400,000 agents, 4 million agents. Those agents are running continuously. They're running in the background."
If the market keeps growing, there should be plenty of room for AMD and Intel to get their piece of the pie.
In a research report earlier this month, Bank of America analyst Vivek Arya once again raised his estimates for the total addressable market (TAM) for server CPUs. A few months ago, Arya expected the TAM to grow by fivefold to $170 billion by 2030.
Now, his new estimate is $210 billion, due to the rise of AI agents.
Nvidia announced stellar second-quarter results, but one number is particularly bad news for some of its chip competitors.
By Bram Berkowitz – Aug 30, 2026 at 11:22AM EST
Nvidia is largely known for its graphics processing units (GPUs), which play a pivotal role in training large language models.
